pages.text: LPG Shortage

LPG Shortage


• The conflict between USA-Israel-Iran has affected the global energy
  supply chain and LPG Shipments from the Persian Gulf to India.

• On 7th March 2026, the central government of India has invoked the
  Essential Commodities Act, 1955 (ECA).

• The Central Government has issued the Natural Gas (Supply
  Regulation) Order, 2026, invoking powers under the ECA. It was
  announced by Cabinet Minister for Petroleum and Natural Gas
  Hardeep Singh Puri.

LPG Shortage

About the Shortage –

• LPG is the main cooking fuel for millions of households across
  India. Ensuring its uninterrupted availability is important because
  any disruption can quickly affect daily life and push up household
  expenses.

• India depends heavily on imports to meet its LPG demand.

• A large portion of these imports comes from the Middle East and
  travels through the Strait of Hormuz which is affected due
  to the USA-Israel-Iran conflict.

LPG Shortage



• At present, about 30% of India’s natural gas requirements are
  routed through the Strait of Hormuz.

• Restaurants, hotels and commercial kitchens in cities such as Delhi,
  Mumbai and Bengaluru have reported difficulty getting commercial
  LPG cylinders, forcing some establishments to scale down operations
  or temporarily shut.

• It has also increased the prices of the domestic LPG prices in India.

LPG Shortage


ECA, 1955 –

• It allows the government to regulate production, supply, and prices
  of essential goods to prevent hoarding, black marketing, and
  shortages.

• Section 3 of the ECA empowers the Central Government to regulate
  the supply and distribution of petroleum and petroleum products and
  related trade for securing their equitable distribution.

• The Act also allows the government to fix price caps and regulate
  trade practices.

LPG Shortage



• In June 2020, the Centre amended the Act to delist certain commodities as
  essential, allowing the government to regulate their supply and prices only
  “under extraordinary circumstances” such as war, famine, extraordinary
  price rise and a natural calamity of grave nature.

• The commodities thus delisted include food items, including cereals,
  pulses, potatoes, onions, edible oilseeds and oils.

• In such cases, limits can be placed on the number of stocks of such items
  held by individuals.

LPG Shortage



• Through Section 5 of the Act, the Central Government can delegate
  its powers to state governments or authorized officers.

• In the recent past the act was invoked during the COVID crisis.

• The government temporarily included masks and hand sanitizers
  under the Essential Commodities framework to prevent shortages
  and ensure that protective medical supplies were sold at affordable
  prices to the public.

LPG Shortage


Natural Gas (Supply Regulation) Order, 2026 –

• Through this order, the centre has created the four-tier priority
  allocation framework. The framework is:
      • Priority Sector I: Domestic PNG, CNG transport, LPG
        production, pipeline fuel.
      • Priority Sector II: Fertilizer Plants – strictly for fertilizer
        production.
      • Priority Sector III: Tea industries, manufacturing, industrial
        consumers.
      • Priority Sector IV: Industrial and Commercial Consumers.

LPG Shortage



• To manage the limited supply, the allocation framework is based on
  consumers' average gas usage over the past six months.

• Gas supplies will be partially or entirely curtailed for non-priority
  industries, including power plants and petrochemical facilities.

• Gas diverted from non-priority to priority sectors will be sold at a
  newly determined pooled price.

LPG Shortage



• Authorities instructed petroleum companies to prioritise
  LPG distribution to domestic consumers to prevent shortages
  that could affect daily cooking fuel requirements of millions of
  households.

• Refineries were prohibited from diverting propane and butane
  streams to petrochemical manufacturing.

• These inputs must be primarily utilised for LPG production to
  maintain sufficient household fuel supply.

LPG Shortage

Other measures taken:

   • 25 day inter-booking period to avoid hoarding/black marketing
     of LPG.

   • Imported LPG is being prioritised to essential non domestic
     sectors such as Hospitals and Educational institutions.

   • A High-level Committee constituted to review supply to other
     non-domestic sectors E.g. hospitality sector.

LPG Shortage

Other measures taken:

   • Entities receiving gas must legally accept the pooled price even if
     it overrides previous contracts, ensuring equitable cost sharing.

   • GAIL (India) Ltd has been tasked with reallocating gas from
     lower-priority users to priority sectors such as domestic PNG,
     CNG, LPG plants and pipeline operations.

LPG Shortage


India’s Position –

• The United States temporarily allowed India to purchase Russian
  crude oil for a period of 30 days.

• India imports more than 60% of its total LPG requirement, making
  domestic supply highly dependent on international markets.

• Nearly 90% of LPG imports come from the Persian Gulf, which
  increases vulnerability to disruptions in this region.

LPG Shortage


• India currently holds only 25–30 days of LPG inventory, creating
  a serious risk of shortage if imports remain disrupted.

• Current Major LNG suppliers: Qatar, United States, Russia,
  Australia. India has begun sourcing spot LPG cargoes from distant
  suppliers such as the United States, Norway and Algeria, which may
  increase supply costs.

• India’s natural gas consumption at present is 195 million metric
  standard cubic metres per day (MMSCMD), of which it imports
  half of its requirements.

NavIC Satellite


• The “positioning data” from the satellite IRNSS-1F stopped coming.
  The atomic clock of the satellite has stopped working.

• However, the satellite will continue to function in-orbit for various
  societal applications to provide one way broadcast messaging
  services.

• The ISRO has informed about the update on March 13.

NavIC Satellite


What is IRNSS –

• In 2006, the project was approved by the Government of India and
  was expected to be completed and implemented by 2015-16.

• Developed by ISRO, IRNSS stands for Indian Regional
  Navigation Satellite System.

• Its operational name is Navigation with Indian Constellation
  (NavIC).

NavIC Satellite

• It is a 7 satellite system which has been operationalised to
  provide positioning data over the Indian subcontinent and
  1500 km around it.

• The constellations' first satellite (IRNSS-1A) was launched on 1st
  July 2013 and the seventh and final satellite (IRNSS-1G) was
  launched on 28th April 2016.

• With the last launch of the constellation's satellite (IRNSS-1G),
  IRNSS was renamed Navigation Indian Constellation (NaVIC) by
  India’s Prime Minister Mr. Narendra Modi in 2016.

NavIC Satellite



• The satellite system has been designed as regional system similar to
  the American GPS.

• It provides navigation or location accuracy till around 10 metres
  over the Indian land and also surrounding countries.

• All the satellites has been placed directly over the Indian region so
  that to provide more accurate navigation.

NavIC Satellite


• Three satellites are placed in Geostationary Orbit (GSO). Four
  satellites are placed in inclined Geosynchronus Orbit (GEO).

• The ground network comprises a control centre, accurate timing
  facility, range and integrity monitoring stations, two-way ranging
  stations, etc.

• IRNSS provides two types of services:
   • Standard Positioning Service (SPS) - that is provided to all
     users.
   • Restricted Service (RS) - an encrypted service provided only
     to authorised users.

NavIC Satellite



• The IRNSS - NavIC project became operational in 2018. NavIC was
  conceived to remove dependence on the satellite systems of other
  countries for navigation, especially for "strategic sectors."

NavIC Satellite

• Each of the seven satellites in the IRNSS constellation weighed
  much less (around 1,425 kg at liftoff).

• They were launched using the lighter Polar Satellite Launch
  Vehicle (PSLV).

• The satellites are: IRNSS-1A (2013); IRNSS-1B (2014); IRNSS-
  1C (2014); IRNSS-1D (2015); IRNSS-1E (2016); IRNSS-1F
  (2016); IRNSS-1G; IRNSS-1H (2017); and IRNSS-1I (2018).

      • IRNSS-1H was launched in 2017 but did not reach the orbit
        because the heat shield protecting the payload failed to open.

NavIC Satellite

What happened now –

• NVS-01 was launched in 2023. After that five satellite in the
  NavIC constellation became capable of providing positioning data:
  IRNSS-1B, IRNSS-1C, IRNSS-1F, IRNSS-1I, and NVS-01.

• These were launched as a new-generation NavIC satellite to provide
  more accurate positioning data.

• The atomic clock of IRNSS-1F has failed recently as notified by
  ISRO. Hence, the satellite can no longer provide positioning data,
  reducing the number of operational satellites in the system.

NavIC Satellite

NVS-02 –

• NVS-02, the second satellite of the new-generation NavIC series
  after NVS-01, was launched in January 2025 aboard GSLV-F15
  during ISRO’s 100th mission and placed in a highly elliptical
  transfer orbit.

• The satellite failed to move into its intended operational orbit due to
  an electrical malfunction that prevented the engine from igniting.

• A review committee found that the signal required to activate the
  pyro valve in the oxidiser line did not reach the engine.

NavIC Satellite

Other Systems in the world –

• The foundation of satellite-based navigation is a global network of
  satellites in medium earth orbit that broadcast radio signals.

• The most developed system is that of the 31 Global Positioning
  System (GPS) satellites, which was developed and operated by
  the United States. It was developed by Department of Defense.

• Three other constellations also provide similar services; together
  these constellations and their respective augmentations are known
  as Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS).

NavIC Satellite

• The other constellations are:

      • GLONASS - It is developed and operated by the Russian
        Federation
      • Galileo - It is developed and operated by the European
        Union
      • BeiDou - It is developed and operated by China.

• India has entered the arena of satellite navigation with its two major
  projects, GAGAN (GPS Aided Geo Augmented Navigation) and
  IRNSS (Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System).

NavIC Satellite
Other Information –

• India also has a GAGAN (GPS Aided Geo Augmented
  Navigation) system.

• GAGAN is a space-based augmentation for GPS developed jointly
  by ISRO and the Airports Authority of India (AAI).

• The GAGAN Signal-In-Space (SIS) is available through GSAT-8 and
  GSAT-10.

• NavIC is recognised by the International Maritime Organisation
  (IMO) as part of the World-Wide Radio Navigation System,
  enabling its use in areas like maritime navigation.

NavIC Satellite


• In 1999 Kargil war, USA denied use of GPS by the Indian military.

• Like India, Japan also has a regional satellite system. QZSS (Quasi-
  Zenith Satellite System) with 4 satellites, mainly augmenting GPS
  over Japan.

• Beidou (China) has over 40 satellites in a mix of medium-earth
  orbit and higher geosynchronous orbits of over 35,000 km.
  India’s all satellites are placed in higher geosynchronous orbits.

NavIC Satellite


• In April 2019, the government made NavIC-based vehicle trackers
  mandatory for all commercial vehicles in the country in
  accordance with the Nirbhaya case verdict.

• Also, Qualcomm Technologies has unveiled mobile chipsets
  supporting NavIC.

• It has been certified by the 3rd Generation Partnership Project
  (3GPP), a global body for coordinating mobile telephony standards.
LS Speaker Removal

LS Speaker Removal


• Lok Sabha rejected the motion to dismiss Lok Sabha Speaker Mr.
  Om Birla on March 11, 2026.

• In February 2026, over 100 MPs submitted a notice seeking removal
  of Mr. Om Birla.

• The reason for removal was "partisan conduct" and the denial of
  permission to the Leader of Opposition (LoP) to speak.

LS Speaker Removal


Procedure for the Removal –

• Article 94 of the Constitution lays down the conditions under which
  the Speaker or Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha may leave office.

• According to Article 94(a), the Speaker or Deputy Speaker
  automatically loses the position if they cease to be a member of the
  Lok Sabha.

• Under Article 94(b), either of them may step down voluntarily by
  submitting a written resignation.

LS Speaker Removal



• Article 94(c) provides that they can be removed through a
  resolution adopted by a majority of all the existing members of
  the House.

• This constitutional provision applies only to the Lok Sabha
  and has no application to the Rajya Sabha.

• The procedure for moving such a resolution is regulated by Rules
  200–203 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business
  in Lok Sabha.

LS Speaker Removal


• A motion for removal can be introduced only after a minimum notice
  period of 14 days. The notice must be submitted in writing to the
  Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha and must bear the signature of
  at least one member.

• If the notice is found to be in order, it is included in the List of
  Business. The presiding officer then reads it before the House.

• For the motion to be taken up for discussion, at least 50 members
  must stand in support. If fewer than 50 members support it, the
  motion fails to obtain the “leave of the House” and is not pursued
  further.

LS Speaker Removal


• The allegations forming the basis of the motion must be precise and
  clearly articulated. The resolution should not include argumentative
  statements, assumptions, sarcasm, personal imputations, or
  defamatory remarks.

• Debate in the House is limited strictly to the charges mentioned in
  the resolution.

• For the motion to succeed, it must secure the support of a
  majority of all the then members of the House, commonly
  referred to as an effective majority.

LS Speaker Removal



• If the resolution is passed with the required majority, the Speaker
  is removed from office with immediate effect.

• Importantly, the Speaker does not vacate the office when the Lok
  Sabha is dissolved. The Speaker continues to hold the position until
  just before the first sitting of the newly constituted Lok Sabha.

• However, if removal occurs through a resolution, the office is
  vacated instantly.

LS Speaker Removal



• When a motion seeking the Speaker’s removal is under
  consideration, the Speaker cannot preside over the House (as
  provided under Article 96).

• Nevertheless, the Speaker is entitled to participate in the
  proceedings and may vote as a regular member.

• However, in the event of a tie, the Speaker cannot exercise a casting
  vote.

LS Speaker Removal

Precedents –

• It has been moved only three times in the history:

      • 1954: Against G.V. Mavalankar (First Speaker).
      • 1966: Against Hukam Singh.
      • 1987: Against Balram Jakhar.

• All three motions failed, and no Speaker has ever been removed
  from office via this process.

LS Speaker Removal

About Om Birla –

• Om Birla was first elected Lok Sabha Speaker in 2019 (17th Lok
  Sabha).

• Later, he was re-elected in 2024 (18th Lok Sabha), becoming the
  first Speaker in 20 years to be re-elected.

• Om Birla represents the Kota–Bundi constituency in Rajasthan in
  the Lok Sabha.

LS Speaker Removal


LS Speaker –

• Elected by the Lok Sabha from among its members; date fixed by the
  President. Holds office for the life of the Lok Sabha and continues even
  after dissolution till the new House meets. The Speaker of the LS is the
  presiding officer and the highest authority of the LS.

• Speaker ensures decorum and prevent disorderly conduct. Speaker has a
  casting vote - Voting only in the case of a tie.

• The Speaker has the final authority to decide if a bill is a Money Bill. It
  decides on disqualification matters under the Tenth Schedule.

LS Speaker Removal


• The Speaker is elected by a simple majority in the House.

• Usually by convention, a member belonging to the ruling party is
  elected Speaker.

      • There are instances when members not belonging to the
        ruling party were elected to the office of the Speaker like
        GMC Balayogi and Manohar Joshi in the 12th and 13th
        Lok Sabha respectively.

• Tenure – It is coterminous with the term of the Lok Sabha that is 5
  years unless he/she resigns or is removed from office before that.

LS Speaker Removal



• The Speaker can also be removed on getting disqualified from being
  a Lok Sabha member under the Representation of the People Act,
  1951.

• A speaker can also tender his resignation to a Deputy Speaker.

• Dr. Neelam Sanjiva Reddy is the only Speaker who resigned from
  the office.

LS Speaker Removal



• The speaker is the final interpreter of the provisions in the following:

   • The Constitution of India
   • The Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business of Lok Sabha
   • The parliamentary precedents, within the House.

• The speaker presides over a joint setting of the two Houses of
  Parliament.

• The speaker appoints the chairman of all the parliamentary
  committees of the Lok Sabha and supervises their functioning.
